title: Hot pull + fill: emergency capacity and GPU replacement retrospective & runbook (draft)
content:
Purpose and scope:

This doc captures a lightweight, actionable runbook for two tightly-coupled scenarios we see frequently: (A) an urgent GPU/node failure that requires physically or logically removing a node (hot pull/replacement) and (B) the fast capacity-fill path (scale-out/backfill) to keep inference pools healthy while replacement occurs. It contains the immediate steps for on-call responders, an ordered checklist for the operator doing the GPU swap, and a short retrospective section with lessons learned from the Nov 2024 incident (INFRA-2314).

Audience:
- Primary: on-call SRE / infra engineer responsible for inference clusters
- Secondary: platform engineers, release managers, solutions engs who coordinate customer impact

Top-level constraints / assumptions:
- Cluster is Kubernetes-based with node groups tagged by instance type and GPU class (e.g., g4dn, a100).
- Running on a cloud provider (AWS/GCP) with ability to reprovision instances, but we also support on-prem processes (separate sections).
- Dedicated pools (customer reserved capacity) must not be autoscaled into without approvals — see "dedicated-pools" annotations.

Preflight (before any destructive action):
1) Announce intent in #sre-imminent (Slack) with incident id and short plan.
2) Create or update a Jira incident (INFRA-XXXX). Link to runbook.
3) Confirm owner and backup: primary operator + second engineer to monitor.
4) Check cluster health dashboard: API request latencies, queue length, token/sec, pod restart rates.
5) Identify affected node(s) and workloads: kubectl get nodes -o wide | grep <node-name> and kubectl describe node <node>. Note pods with pod disruption budgets (PDBs) and stateful sets.

Immediate mitigation (5–15m):
- If node exhibiting GPU hardware errors but still responds: kubectl cordon <node> to prevent new pods.
- If safe to evict: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force (use --grace-period=120 for faster)
- For pods that won't evict due to PDBs or local storage: annotate node with sre/evacuate=no and escalate to app owner; if that blocks, consider emergency fallback routes (traffic reroute to other regions or serving variants).
- If node is completely unresponsive: mark node as NotReady and proceed to reprovision in cloud console; skip drain step.

Commands (cheat-sheet):
- Check node & GPU drivers: kubectl describe node <node> | egrep -i "gpu|nvidia|taints|conditions"
- Cordon: kubectl cordon <node>
- Drain: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force
- Quick evict of single pod: kubectl delete pod <pod> --grace-period=30
- Label to prevent autoscaler: kubectl label node <node> sre/repair=in-progress --overwrite
- Remove node from load balancer (provider): aws elbv2 deregister-targets --target-group-arn <arn> --targets Id=<instance-id>  OR gcloud compute instance-groups managed set-instance-template <ig> --instances <instance>

Safety-net: preserving customer SLAs
- If PDBs prevent safe eviction, escalate immediately (Slack @oncall-platform) and enable fallback routing.
- For inference-critical routes, automatically switch to a compatible model variant in another pool (see routing fallback policy). Ensure routing-tracer is enabled before action.

GPU replacement path (physical/node reprovision):
A) Cloud reprovision (preferred):
- Mark node unschedulable (cordon) and drain as above.
- Terminate or stop the instance in cloud console (AWS/GCP).
- Confirm autoscaler / instance group will provision a replacement with same labels. If not, manually spin a new instance from the correct launch template.
- Verify node boots, kubelet joins, GPU drivers load (ssh into node, run nvidia-smi).
- Remove repair label and uncordon once healthy: kubectl label node <node> sre/repair- && kubectl uncordon <node>.

B) On-prem / rack-level GPU swap (physical hardware):
- Safety: power down host (follow DC SOP), order parts (spare-pool part id: SP-GPU-300).
- Swap GPU following vendor guide; ensure ECC and firmware versions match.
- Boot node into maintenance image, run driver reinstall script: /opt/redwood/scripts/reinstall-gpu-drivers.sh
- Run functional test: run bench-infer --model small --batch 1 --warmup 50 and check latency and mem usage.
- If tests pass, bring node back into cluster (uncordon).

Fast capacity fill (fill path) — when replacing nodes will take >10m:
- Option A (autoscaler): increase desired count on instance group by +N (based on active queue/backlog). Do not scale dedicated pools without approval.
- Option B (burst pool): provision instances from burst pool (cheaper/less secure) with automatic routing. Use tag "burst=true".
- Option C (fallback routing): switch high-latency-tolerant routes to lower-tier models in unaffected pools.

Capacity scaling commands (cheat-sheet):
- AWS ASG: aws autoscaling set-desired-capacity --auto-scaling-group-name <asg> --desired-capacity <n>
- GCP MIG: gcloud compute instance-groups managed resize <mig-name> --size <n> --zone <z>
- Kubernetes nodepool annotation to accept burst: kubectl annotate nodepool <pool> redwood/burst-allowed=true

Post-action validation (0–30m after changes):
- Confirm pods rescheduled: kubectl get pods -o wide --field-selector=status.phase!=Running
- Check model endpoints: curl health endpoints and sample inference run for 3 routes with expected latencies.
- Dashboard: check per-route latency and token rate; cost/throughput alerts should be suppressed when filling is deliberate.

Rollback criteria (undo fast-fill or new node):
- If replacement node fails health checks (nvidia-smi errors, kubelet flapping, failing bench-infer), terminate and roll back ASG/MIG change.
- If autoscaling caused capacity to bleed into dedicated pools (policy violation), immediately reduce desired count and notify sales/CS.

Retrospective notes from INFRA-2314 (Nov 2024) — quick lessons:
- Root cause: intermittent PCIe ECC errors on a subset of A100 hosts after firmware update.
- What worked: cordon+drain + autoscale fill kept 95% of traffic within latency SLO for 30 minutes.
- What didn't: PDBs for a stateful reranker blocked eviction of 3 pods; we lacked a fast app-owner on-call contact and forced an emergency manual failover.
- Action items (owners in parens):
  - Add a golden-test for driver firmware compatibility in preflight (Miguel).
  - Add a short-circuit policy to allow controlled eviction of PDB-protected pods under emergency (SRE-789) (Jordan + Product).
  - Maintain a modest spare-node pool in each region to avoid cross-region fallbacks (Asha).

Open questions / TODOs:
- Should we automate node labelling for repair window to integrate with autoscaler? (Yes, prototype in infra repo).
- Define exact thresholds for automatic capacity fill vs manual approval (latency > X ms for Y minutes).
- Document full customer-notification template for Dedicated customers.

Appendix: quick links and scripts
- repair helper: /opt/redwood/tools/node-repair.sh --node <node> (runs driver checks, labels node)
- bench script: /opt/redwood/tools/bench-infer.sh --model tiny --requests 50
- Incident template: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/SRE/Incident+Template
- Slack: #sre-imminent, #oncall-platform (use @oncall-sre when escalation needed)

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep this doc intentionally terse; separate deeper playbooks for on-prem swap and vendor RMA.
- After next oncall rotation, run a 30-minute drill: cordon+drain 1 node in staging and exercise autoscaler + backfill. Capture timings.

Status: draft — needs review from platform eng and solutions eng (routing fallbacks).

Contact: Priya Desai (oncall lead), paged via #sre-imminent.
